clue.text: Height ratio distorted power of the Montgolfiers

indicators.note: something distorted is twisted out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warped proportion of height seems to describe the lifting force of an early balloon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distorted' rearranges H plus RATIO. The Montgolfier brothers flew the first manned hot-air balloon in 1783.
explanation.definitionFit: Heated air was literally what lifted the Montgolfier balloons, giving their motive force.

clue.text: With which one sees far via close, endlessly blending

indicators.note: blending mixes things together, so these letters are combined in a new order
endlessly means the word close loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A description of glasses that let the wearer see near and far, merging one into the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' cuts CLOSE to CLOS; 'blending' rearranges FAR, VIA and CLOS.
explanation.definitionFit: Multifocal spectacle lenses are a means by which a wearer sees at every distance.

clue.text: One Cheshire banker, absorbed by Hereford's, died astonished

indicators.note: absorbed by means taken inside the following river's name

parts.note: Hereford stands on the River Wye
I is the Roman numeral for one
a banker is a river; the Dee flows past Chester in Cheshire

explanation.surface: Someone from Cheshire, swallowed up by a Hereford crowd, dies of amazement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' is a crossword word for a river (it has banks); the rivers here are British: the Dee in Cheshire, the Wye at Hereford.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone astonished stares with eyes opened wide, so the phrase is an idiom for amazement.

clue.text: "Goody-goody! Good time!" (Homer)

parts.note: pi is slang for pious, a goody-goody
an eon is a vast stretch of time

explanation.surface: An exclamation of delight attributed to the poet Homer, or perhaps to Homer Simpson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homer' suggests the Greek poet; it is a homing bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A homer is a homing bird trained to return to its loft, a racing variety of this bird.

clue.text: Something from the kitchen garden: "Pressure different bees!"

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
different means other
bees read as letters is B's, the letter B twice

explanation.surface: A gardener exclaims about a strange sort of bee buzzing in the vegetable patch.
explanation.definitionFit: Leafy plants such as kale or chard grown for cooking are a typical crop of a vegetable plot.

clue.text: Bargain lot

definitions.meaning: a bargain is something bought at a fine price
a lot means a large amount

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses: a bargain bought cheaply, and a great quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both a fine bargain and a large amount, two everyday senses.

clue.text: Bard of Welsh salient, I gathered

indicators.note: gathered suggests material pulled together and folded, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Welsh bard is pictured collecting a prominent military position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathered' rearranges SALIENT plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixth-century poet named here is one of the earliest bards of the Welsh tradition.

clue.text: Don't go to s-sleep

parts.note: the stammered s gives a letter S
kip is British slang for sleep

explanation.surface: Someone stammers an instruction to stay put and fall asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter supplies S; KIP is everyday British slang for a nap.
explanation.definitionFit: To miss or omit attending something is to fail to go to it, a common informal sense.

clue.text: Victory for her folks up East

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: folks means one's family, kin

explanation.surface: A woman's family rises in the east and triumphs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns KIN round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of triumph is personified victory, hence 'for her'.

clue.text: Hard worker, given time, managed to collar Simpson

indicators.note: to collar means to grab round the neck, so one piece goes around another

parts.note: managed means ran, as a business
O.J. Simpson, the American footballer

explanation.surface: A diligent worker, sentenced to time, helps to arrest a man named Simpson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to collar' is the containment signal. O.J. Simpson was a famous American football star.
explanation.definitionFit: Working like a soldier of ancient Troy is an idiom for working tirelessly.

clue.text: An ode from the third man, a Yank: a Cafe boss in old Casablanca

parts.note: Harry Lime, the American villain of the film The Third Man

parts.words: a Cafe boss in old Casablanca
parts.note: Rick runs Rick's Cafe in the film Casablanca

explanation.surface: Film buffs might link Harry Lime and Rick Blaine, two classic movie men.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces come from classic films: Harry Lime in The Third Man (1949), and Rick Blaine of Rick's Cafe in Casablanca (1942).
explanation.definitionFit: Calling a five-line comic verse an ode is playful, since both are poems, though one is light.

clue.text: Old, wretched Conservative twice removed from the list

parts.note: ex means former, old
dire means wretched
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
Tory is the everyday name for a Conservative

explanation.surface: An old, miserable Tory politician is struck off a membership roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative twice' gives the party twice over: C and TORY. Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A phone number kept out of the published book is unlisted, the British term for this.

clue.text: Where anything's possible with PC? Yes! Caber-tossing!

indicators.note: tossing throws things about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: An excited computer user cheers about being able to try a Highland caber toss online.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossing' rearranges PC, YES and CABER. Tossing the caber is a Scottish Highland Games event.
explanation.definitionFit: The online virtual world is a realm where any imagined thing can be made to exist.

clue.text: BBC by radio destroyed: a tragedy!

indicators.note: by radio means broadcast, so heard rather than read

parts.note: Auntie is the British nickname for the BBC
destroyed means gone

explanation.surface: Someone laments that the national broadcaster has been wiped out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by radio' turns AUNTIE, the British nickname for the BBC, into its sound-alike ANTI.
explanation.definitionFit: This play by Sophocles is one of the best-known Greek tragedies.

clue.text: Capital of High Priest to accept lapse? Capital!

indicators.note: capital of means the first letter, the capital, of the next word
to accept means taking another piece inside

parts.note: Eli is the high priest in the Book of Samuel
to sink is to lapse, as into decline

explanation.surface: A high priest is asked to tolerate a fall from grace, and the reaction is a delighted cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' appears twice: first as the first-letter signal, then as the definition, a nation's chief city.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is the seat of government of Finland, a national capital.

clue.text: Here hopeful dippers filled bath from barrels

definitions.text: Here hopeful dippers filled bath from barrels

parts.words: Here hopeful dippers filled bath from barrels
parts.note: a lucky-dip container at a fete, a large tub filled with cereal husks into which hopeful children plunge their hands for prizes

explanation.surface: Bathers dip hopefully into a tub filled from barrels.
explanation.walkthrough: A British fete game: a tub full of cereal husks, with small prizes buried in it for children to dig out.
explanation.definitionFit: This lucky dip is a tub of husks where people reach in hoping to pull out a prize.

clue.text: Vintner departed sorry mess for box consumer

indicators.note: a sorry mess is a jumble, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for died or departed

explanation.surface: A wine merchant has left behind a dreadful muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorry mess' rearranges VINTNER plus D. 'Box' is slang for the television.
explanation.definitionFit: A ready meal on a tray is eaten in front of the television, so it is food for a viewer.

clue.text: How pasta should be 'eld out before wrapping

indicators.note: wrapping means going around another piece

parts.note: ante is Latin for before

indicators.note: out means disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Cookery advice: pasta should be held out before being wrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges 'ELD, which is held with its H dropped as a Cockney might say it; 'wrapping' is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for to the tooth, the phrase describes pasta cooked to be firm when bitten.

clue.text: Herein Knopfler once starred, is it not right?

definitions.text: Herein Knopfler once starred, is it not right?

indicators.note: not right means wrongly ordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rock fan asks whether a famous guitarist once played in this band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not right' rearranges STARRED IS IT. Mark Knopfler fronted this British rock band.
explanation.definitionFit: Mark Knopfler was the guitarist and singer of this rock band, so he starred in it.

clue.text: One horn's enough for these ungulates

definitions.text: One horn's enough for these ungulates

parts.words: One horn's enough for these ungulates
parts.note: hoofed beasts such as the Indian and Javan species manage with a single nose horn

explanation.surface: Some hoofed animals need only one horn.
explanation.definitionFit: These large hoofed mammals bear nose horns, and some species have just one.

clue.text: Songs around this before the Ashes?

definitions.text: Songs around this before the Ashes?

parts.words: Songs around this before the Ashes?
parts.note: scouts sing round an outdoor blaze, which burns before it becomes ashes; the Ashes also suggest cricket

explanation.surface: Fans sing together on the eve of an England-Australia cricket series.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the cricket series between England and Australia, a misdirection from the embers a blaze leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: An outdoor blaze at a camp is where people traditionally gather to sing.

clue.text: See 20
There's always one! A wine-growing valley in Cyprus

parts.note: ay is an old word for always
I is the Roman numeral for one
Napa Valley in California is famed for wine

explanation.surface: A remark about a Californian-style wine valley turning up on a Mediterranean island.
explanation.walkthrough: AY (also spelt aye) is an old poetic word meaning ever.
explanation.definitionFit: This holiday resort town lies on the south-east coast of the island of Cyprus.

clue.text: This culture's a lot of bull? No! I'm an idiot!

definitions.text: This culture's a lot of bull?

indicators.note: an idiot is a muddled fool, so the letters are muddled too

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a culture as nonsense and then calls themselves a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'idiot' rearranges NO plus I'M AN. The culture of ancient Crete was famous for bull-leaping and the Minotaur, so 'bull' is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bronze Age civilisation of Crete revered bulls, as the myth of the Minotaur shows.

clue.text: Bonnie Prince Charlie's affectation?

parts.note: Charles Edward Stuart, called the Young Pretender, laid claim to the throne; a word for affectation also names a claim

explanation.surface: A question about the Jacobite prince's mannerisms.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonnie Prince Charlie, the Young Pretender, claimed the British throne in 1745.
explanation.definitionFit: An affectation is a false show, and the word also means a claim such as a pretender makes.

clue.text: Permit one to run from fleshy smell of mushrooms

indicators.note: to run from means these pieces follow on after the next

parts.note: BO is body odour, a smell of the flesh
to let is to permit
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Allow someone to flee the meaty odour of mushrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to run from' places the permitting and the one after the smell; BO is body odour.
explanation.definitionFit: These are a genus of fleshy fungi with pores, including the cep or porcino.
